title: Kubernetes Storage Handbook: Volumes, PV, PVC, StorageClass & CSI
summary: A page-by-page study series on how Kubernetes gives pods durable storage — from ephemeral volumes and the PV/PVC binding contract to StorageClasses, dynamic provisioning, CSI drivers, volume expansion, snapshots and StatefulSet storage. Covers mechanics, YAML examples, trade-offs, failure modes and a final cheatsheet.

chapters.title: Kubernetes Storage
points: Container filesystems are ephemeral: writes to the container layer vanish on restart, not just on delete
A pod is the unit of storage sharing — containers in one pod can mount the same volume
Three layers of the model: Volume (pod-scoped), PersistentVolume (cluster resource), PersistentVolumeClaim (namespaced request)
StorageClass turns manual PV creation into dynamic provisioning
CSI (Container Storage Interface) is the plug-in contract every modern storage vendor implements
Storage is the hardest part of stateful workloads: nodes are cattle, disks are not
What this handbook covers: volume types, PV lifecycle, access modes, binding, reclaim policies, StorageClass, CSI architecture, expansion, snapshots, StatefulSets, mistakes, cheatsheet
Prerequisites: pods, deployments, kubectl basics

chapters.title: Volumes: Storage That Lives With the Pod
points: Definition: a Volume is a directory, backed by some medium, accessible to containers in a pod; its lifetime is the pod's lifetime, not the container's
Container restart keeps volume data; pod deletion destroys it (for ephemeral types)
Declared under `spec.volumes`, consumed per container via `volumeMounts.mountPath`
emptyDir: scratch space created empty when the pod is scheduled; `medium: Memory` makes it a tmpfs that counts against the container memory limit
hostPath: mounts a node directory into the pod — node-affine, a security risk, mostly for node agents like log shippers
configMap / secret / downwardAPI / projected: read-only volumes that inject data, not storage
Example: sidecar log pattern — app writes /var/log to an emptyDir, sidecar reads the same emptyDir
`subPath` mounts one file or subdirectory instead of the whole volume; `subPathExpr` expands env vars like the pod name
Mounting a volume over a non-empty container directory hides the original contents
Ephemeral inline volumes (`ephemeral.volumeClaimTemplate`) get PVC semantics with pod lifetime

chapters.title: PersistentVolume: The Cluster's Piece of Disk
points: Definition: a PV is a cluster-scoped resource representing a real piece of storage, provisioned by an admin or dynamically by a driver
PV is not namespaced — it has no namespace and is claimed by exactly one PVC at a time
Key spec fields: `capacity.storage`, `accessModes`, `persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy`, `storageClassName`, `volumeMode`, and the driver source (`csi`, `nfs`, `local`, …)
volumeMode: `Filesystem` (default, formatted and mounted) vs `Block` (raw device at `volumeDevices`) for databases that manage their own layout
Phases: Available, Bound, Released, Failed — Released means the PVC is gone but the data has not been reclaimed
Reclaim policies: Delete (destroy the backing volume), Retain (keep data, PV stuck Released until an admin acts), Recycle (deprecated, removed)
Static provisioning example: a YAML PV with an NFS server and path, matched by a claim
`nodeAffinity` on a PV pins it to nodes that can actually reach it — mandatory for `local` volumes
PV capacity is a matching hint, not an enforced quota — the backing disk defines the real size
Finalizer `kubernetes.io/pv-protection` blocks deletion while a PV is bound

chapters.title: PersistentVolumeClaim and the Binding Contract
points: Definition: a PVC is a namespaced request for storage — size, access mode, class — that the control plane satisfies with a PV
The PV/PVC split mirrors node/pod: the claim is the abstraction that lets an app author ignore the storage backend
Binding: the PV controller matches a Pending PVC to an Available PV with sufficient capacity, compatible accessModes and equal storageClassName; the match is exclusive and one-to-one
A PVC can bind to a larger PV than requested — the extra capacity is wasted, never split
Pods reference a claim by name: `volumes: [{name: data, persistentVolumeClaim: {claimName: pgdata}}]`; pod and PVC must be in the same namespace
A PVC stays Pending forever if no PV matches and no StorageClass can provision one — `kubectl describe pvc` shows the reason
`volumeName` on a PVC forces a specific PV; `selector` matches PV labels for static pools
`kubernetes.io/pvc-protection` finalizer keeps a PVC alive while a pod uses it, so deleting a PVC in use just marks it Terminating
Deleting a Deployment does not delete its PVCs — that is a feature and a cost surprise
Example: full YAML of PVC + Deployment mounting it, plus `kubectl get pvc,pv` output read line by line

chapters.title: Access Modes and Volume Topology
points: ReadWriteOnce (RWO): mountable read-write by pods on a single node — the default for block storage like EBS or a GCE PD
ReadOnlyMany (ROX): many nodes may mount it read-only
ReadWriteMany (RWX): many nodes read-write — needs a shared filesystem (NFS, CephFS, EFS, Azure Files), not a block device
ReadWriteOncePod (RWOP): exactly one pod cluster-wide may use it — the real mutual-exclusion guarantee, CSI-only
RWO means one *node*, not one pod: several pods on the same node can share an RWO volume, which surprises people who expected locking
Access modes are a scheduling contract, not enforcement — the driver decides what actually happens on a double mount
Comparison row: block volume (RWO, fast, single-attach) vs file share (RWX, slower, POSIX quirks) vs object storage (not a volume at all)
volumeBindingMode `Immediate` binds at claim time and can pin a pod to the wrong zone; `WaitForFirstConsumer` delays binding until a pod is scheduled
Topology labels (`topology.kubernetes.io/zone`) let the scheduler and driver agree on where the disk can live
Multi-attach error: `Multi-Attach error for volume ... Volume is already exclusively attached to one node` during rolling updates of RWO workloads
Fix pattern: use `Recreate` strategy or a StatefulSet instead of a RollingUpdate Deployment on an RWO volume

chapters.title: StorageClass and Dynamic Provisioning
points: Definition: a StorageClass is a named profile of storage — provisioner plus parameters — that lets PVCs create PVs on demand
Mechanism: PVC names a class, the external-provisioner sees the Pending claim, calls CreateVolume on the driver, then creates and binds the PV automatically
Fields: `provisioner`, `parameters` (driver-specific: type, iops, fsType, encrypted), `reclaimPolicy`, `allowVolumeExpansion`, `volumeBindingMode`, `mountOptions`, `allowedTopologies`
The default class is marked by annotation `storageclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class: "true"`; a PVC with no `storageClassName` uses it
`storageClassName: ""` (empty string) disables dynamic provisioning and forces static matching — different from omitting the field
Example: a gp3 class with `type: gp3`, `iops: "6000"`, `allowVolumeExpansion: true`, `volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer`
Classes are immutable in practice — most fields cannot be edited; create a new class and migrate
Reclaim policy is inherited from the class at provisioning time, and the default is Delete — deleting a PVC destroys the data
Common pattern: tiered classes (fast-ssd, standard, cheap-cold) so app teams pick by name, not by backend
Two default classes, or none, is a common cluster misconfiguration that leaves claims Pending or in the wrong tier
Trade-off: static provisioning gives control and pre-existing data; dynamic gives self-service and less toil

chapters.title: CSI: How Storage Drivers Actually Plug In
points: Definition: CSI is a vendor-neutral gRPC specification so storage vendors ship out-of-tree drivers instead of patching Kubernetes
Why it exists: in-tree volume plugins forced vendor code into the kubelet and kube-controller-manager; the CSI migration moved them out and the legacy plugins were removed

Three gRPC services: Identity (who am I, capabilities), Controller (CreateVolume, DeleteVolume, ControllerPublishVolume/attach, CreateSnapshot), Node (NodeStageVolume, NodePublishVolume, NodeUnpublish)
Deployment shape: a controller Deployment (driver + sidecars) plus a node DaemonSet (driver + node-driver-registrar) talking over a UNIX socket

Sidecars are the glue: external-provisioner watches PVCs, external-attacher creates VolumeAttachments, external-resizer handles expansion, external-snapshotter handles snapshots, livenessprobe reports health
Attach vs mount: ControllerPublish attaches the device to the node, NodeStage formats and mounts it once per node, NodePublish bind-mounts it into each pod's directory
CSIDriver object declares behavior: `attachRequired`, `podInfoOnMount`, `fsGroupPolicy`, `volumeLifecycleModes`
CSINode object records which drivers a node runs and its topology keys
Ephemeral CSI inline volumes let drivers like secrets-store mount data with no PVC at all
Debug path: `kubectl get volumeattachment`, then the external-attacher logs, then the node driver logs on the target node
Example: `kubectl get csidrivers` output and reading a VolumeAttachment to see a stuck attach

chapters.title: Expansion, Snapshots and Cloning
points: Volume expansion: edit `spec.resources.requests.storage` on the PVC; the class must set `allowVolumeExpansion: true`
Two-stage resize: the controller grows the backing volume (ControllerExpandVolume), then the kubelet grows the filesystem (NodeExpandVolume) — watch `status.capacity` not `spec`
Online expansion works on most modern CSI drivers; older ones need the pod restarted to finish the filesystem step
Shrinking is not supported — the only path down is a new smaller volume plus a data copy
VolumeSnapshot, VolumeSnapshotContent and VolumeSnapshotClass mirror the PVC/PV/StorageClass triple for point-in-time copies
Restore: create a PVC with `dataSource` pointing at a VolumeSnapshot; the new volume must be at least as large as the snapshot
Cloning: `dataSource` referencing another PVC copies a live volume, same class and same namespace only
Snapshots are crash-consistent, not application-consistent — quiesce or use the database's own backup for a transactional guarantee
Snapshots usually live in the storage backend, not in the cluster — deleting the namespace does not necessarily delete billed snapshots
The snapshot CRDs and snapshot-controller are add-ons: they are not installed by default on a bare cluster
Example: expand a PVC from 20Gi to 50Gi and verify with `kubectl get pvc -o jsonpath='{.status.capacity.storage}'`

chapters.title: StatefulSets and Per-Pod Storage
points: Deployments share one PVC across replicas; StatefulSets give each pod its own via `volumeClaimTemplates`
Naming is deterministic: `<template>-<statefulset>-<ordinal>`, e.g. `data-postgres-0`, so a rescheduled pod reattaches its exact disk
Stable network identity plus stable storage identity is what makes databases and quorum systems work
PVCs from a StatefulSet survive scale-down and deletion by default — scaling back up reuses the old data
`persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicy` (whenDeleted / whenScaled) finally lets you opt into automatic cleanup
With WaitForFirstConsumer, each replica's volume is provisioned in the zone where its pod lands, spreading a cluster across AZs
Local persistent volumes give raw-disk speed but pin the pod to one node — a node loss is a data loss unless the app replicates
Comparison: replicate at the app layer (Postgres streaming, Cassandra) vs replicate at the storage layer (Ceph, cloud disks) — do not pay for both without reason
Example: a 3-replica StatefulSet with a 100Gi volumeClaimTemplate on a fast-ssd class
Backup is not a snapshot schedule alone — restore has to be rehearsed, including PVC recreation

chapters.title: Failure Modes, Permissions and Cost
points: PVC Pending: no matching PV, wrong class name, zone mismatch, or the provisioner pod is down — always read `kubectl describe pvc` events first
Pod stuck ContainerCreating with `FailedMount ... timed out waiting for the condition`: attach or mount failure, check the node kubelet and CSI node logs
`Multi-Attach error`: an RWO volume still attached to an old node, common when a node goes NotReady and the pod is rescheduled
Permission denied on mount: the container runs as non-root but the volume is root-owned — set `securityContext.fsGroup` so the kubelet chowns the volume
`fsGroupChangePolicy: OnRootMismatch` avoids a recursive chown that can take minutes on volumes with millions of files
A terminating PVC that never goes away is a finalizer waiting on a pod; find the consumer instead of force-removing the finalizer
Retain + delete-the-PVC leaves a Released PV that will never rebind until `spec.claimRef` is cleared
Full disk symptoms: `No space left on device`, evicted pods from ephemeral-storage pressure — emptyDir and container logs count against node ephemeral storage
Set `ephemeral-storage` requests and limits, and `sizeLimit` on emptyDir, so one pod cannot fill a node
Cost trap: orphaned PVs, unused snapshots and over-provisioned IOPS keep billing after the workload is gone
Quota control: `requests.storage` and per-class `<class>.storageclass.storage.k8s.io/requests.storage` in a ResourceQuota

chapters.title: Kubernetes Storage Cheatsheet
points: Object map: Volume (pod lifetime) → PVC (namespaced request) → PV (cluster resource) → StorageClass (provisioning profile) → CSI driver (implementation)
Access modes: RWO = one node, ROX = many read-only, RWX = shared filesystem, RWOP = one pod cluster-wide
Reclaim policies: Delete = data gone with the PVC, Retain = data kept and the PV needs manual cleanup
Binding modes: Immediate = bind now and risk a zone mismatch, WaitForFirstConsumer = bind where the pod schedules
`storageClassName` unset = default class; `""` = no dynamic provisioning
Commands: `kubectl get pvc,pv,sc`, `kubectl describe pvc <name>`, `kubectl get volumeattachment`, `kubectl get csidrivers`, `kubectl get volumesnapshot`
Expand: patch `spec.resources.requests.storage`, confirm via `status.capacity`; never try to shrink
Snapshot restore: PVC with `dataSource: {kind: VolumeSnapshot}`; clone: `dataSource: {kind: PersistentVolumeClaim}`
Non-root pods: set `fsGroup`; large volumes: add `fsGroupChangePolicy: OnRootMismatch`
Stateful apps: StatefulSet + volumeClaimTemplates + WaitForFirstConsumer + a retention policy
Debug order: PVC events → StorageClass and provisioner logs → VolumeAttachment → node CSI DaemonSet logs → kubelet
Rules of thumb: default to dynamic provisioning, Retain for anything you would cry over, RWX only when the app truly needs it, and rehearse the restore
